by Senator Frelinghuysen, Republican, New Jersey, as a new autocracy tending toward Bolshevism.

Criticising the demands of the bituminous coal miners for a five day week and increased wages, Senator the senate committee investigating the coal strike, called upon American public opinion to scotch a movement which he feared would result in class government.

The New Jersey senator said the demands of the miners, half of them aliens, were "inordinate" and could not be granted, as they would result in decreased production and an increase in price to the consumer from $2.50 to $3.50 a ton.

Is the United States ready to be dictated to by these men? he asked.

"The time has come to put an end to this new autocracy," said the senator. "Unless this intolerable condition can be rectified, unless some means can be found to prevent imposition of such unthinkable demands and penalties, unless collective bargaining can be continued in an orderly manner and with due regard to the public welfare and comfort, a new remedy must be applied—the remedy of making labor amenable to the same extent as capital to the laws of the United States.

Referring to the steel strike, the New York pressmen's strike and other labor disturbances, Senator Frelinghuysen said:

"Where is this striking frenzy to stop? Unless a halt is called we shall reach a state of anarchy infinitely worse than the autocracy of Germany. This is class government and not democracy.

"There is determined movement throughout the land to assume control of all government functions in behalf of a class," continued Senator Frelinghuysen. "We have come to a parting of the ways. This country is not ready to be dictated to by a horde of aliens. Any citizen who seeks to advance the interest of himself and his associates at the expense of general public is not a patriotic citizen. Sovietism means class rule. We cannot permit that in America.

Labor Must Not Abuse Power.

Labor unionism should be upheld for one primary principle: to obtain and maintain justice for the man who earns his bread by the sweat of his brow, but when the power of organization is employed to impose injustice against all other classes of society, the law of the land should be invoked to prevent the abuse of such."

cluded, however, that such action must in-
volve the real absorption of securities by
the American public. The securities may
be of a kind issued by foreign enterprises
and resold here, or they may be the result
of local financing in which American banks
will participate so that the American in-
vestor gets the benefit of a guarantee fur-
nished by domestic institutions which he
knows. However the value of the issues
may be safeguarded, the point is that they
are attractive. This is no time for recurrence
of extravagance, but it is already apparent
that such tendency exists, and that it will
make itself manifest unless checked. The
reason for checking it is that the banks
of the country cannot be expected to carry
the load of European support pending the
time when European business men get into
position to take care of themselves. In-
doubtedly whatever plan is adopted will,
therefore, give rise to some very attractive
offerings of securities. The investor who
has a little money to spare will be able
to do better for himself than for a good
while past. Now that much of the cream
has been skinned off from stocks, it may
easily be that the market for bonds or notes
will offer the next best opening to the
prudent man with money who prefers cer-
tainty to a hazard.


Gold and Prices


The desirability of providing moderately
for the financing of our export trade, and
at the same time of absorbing some very
attractive securities by the exercise of a
little thrift ought to be obvious to investors
who have been well trained
during the time of the war.
We do not want commodity prices to go
much higher than they at present, yet
they will certainly do so if we continue
to spend our savings in making demand
at the same time trying to buy. Particularly will this
be true if we insist on getting paid in gold
for the balance that is due us. Since the
gold embargo taken off, we have lost
some yellow metal, although hardly enough
to offset our recent gains from domestic
production and importations. Prices are
rising both here and in England, as the cur-
rent index numbers show and the need for
saving is again emphasized both by high
rates for money and good returns on invest-
ments, unusual values for stocks and real
estate and demands for funds for foreign
financing. All influences seem to combine
to urge upon the individual the desirability
of thrift and the careful investment of his
funds in some of the forms now so numerous
that cannot help paying him good returns.

sacrificed. We have given our hus-
bands, sons, and sweethearts, some
never to return, and we have given
willingly. We worked in the Red Cross
and other organizations. We have
practiced economies we have never
even dreamed of. We have Liberty
bonds, War Saving Stamps, in fact we
lived up to the splendid American
spirit, but we cannot, even in part,
begin to realize the meaning of sacri-
fice during the war as our sisters over
the sea have."

Mrs. Gill, whose home is in Chicago,
like thousands of other American
women, felt the desire to assist in
any way that she might on the bloody
battlefield over there and in the devas-
tated regions. She sailed from New
York not long after the outbreak of
the war, under the auspices of the
American Red Cross.

Assisting in the hospital and in car-
ing for refugees from Belgium, Mrs.
Gill came home for a period of rest
and was on the high seas when decla-
ration of war was made by the Unit-
ed States. After a short time she
again returned to Europe.

"With few and small organizations
at the beginning of the war to care
for the wounded, etc., it was wonderful
in what a short time England and
France soon had splendidly equipped
hospitals, canteens, etc.," she said.
"Having been there in the beginning, I
was more impressed with the splendid
work accomplished in this line on my
arrival the second time.

"The Red Cross, Salvation Army, X.
of C., and other organizations accom-
plished wonderful work over there
and are still doing so, but I should
like to make special mention of the
splendid work accomplished by the Y.
M. C. A., especially during the first
part of the war. Their huts seemed
to spring up overnight as it were.
Something I, as an American, was
proud to note was the American ambu-
lance hospital in France, one of the
most completely equipped and up to
date hospitals there. It was opened
at the beginning of the war, begun by
fund from Harvard and kept up by
voluntary contributions from Ameri-

the shattered and maimed of the

in farming, but is at present liv-
ing at 325 T. street, Tacoma, and
is employed at the Todd ship
yards, while talking to a Tanlac
representative the other day.

Mr. Lewis, "I went up to Roberts,
Idaho, and while working on my
homestead noticed that I was
falling in strength and health. I
was losing weight and getting
weaker day by day. This condition
kept me for the whole time I was
there, and at the end of the year
I was almost a complete wreck. I
had no appetite and the climate
there seemed to affect my breath-
ing. Finally got to where I would
have to get out of bed at night
and walk around in the yard for
hours at a time in order to get
good breath. My physician told me
that I would have to get out of
that climate or could not possibly
live much longer. Then I gave up
the homestead and came back to
Tacoma, and when I got back here
I was simply down and out in my
health.

friend of mine told me about Tan-
lac and advised me to give it a
trial, and after taking a couple of
bottles of it I felt so much better
that I actually went to work doing
hard labor like handling brick and
steel. My appetite came back, and
from that day to this, it just seems
I can't get enough to eat. I have
no trouble in breathing now, and
can go to bed at night and sleep
right through without a break in
time to get up in the morning.

pound a week ever since. I am
as well and strong now as I ever
was and am still swinging to my
job at the shipyards and my work
doesn't hurt me at all. Yes, sir,
Tanlac is the best medicine I have
ever seen, and expect to keep it
on hand as long as I live."

U. S. Troops on Guard.

Chicago. July 4.—While the officials of the government, state and city were optimistic that today would pass without event, precautions had been taken to act quickly and effectively should there be any demonstration toward fulfillment of threat of an outbreak by radicals.

Two companies of the Fourteenth United States Infantry were stationed in the city and state militia had been ordered to hold itself in readiness. In every station the reserves were concentrated with orders to remain until 5 o'clock Monday morning.
